To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the credit based CME systems have been developed by the Medical Royal College without reference to adult learning principles, without a clear rationale, and with no evaluation of their impact on doctors' continuing learning.

(1) credit based CME systems are not necessarily the best way to promote continuing education for doctors and (2) doctors' professional development is best supported by a variety of approaches to learning, including the development of a personal portfolio of learning.

1) the CME system has had a negative effect on the learning culture of the medical profession in the UK; and 2) the CME systems have been imposed on the profession by the Medical Royal College and have been accepted as a bureaucratic convenience rather than an educational necessity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the bureaucratic and professional aspects of continuing professional development.
the impact of bureaucratic CME systems and the extent to which they can be reconciled with the principles of professional development.
the relationship between professional learning and bureaucratic convenience in the medical professions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no evidence that the current CME system in the United Kingdom is achieving its objectives of promoting the continuing development of the profession, nor of providing an appropriate and efficient means for monitoring and evaluating doctors' continuing education.
the credit based CME systems are not a satisfactory way to promote continuing professional development.
there are no simple answers to the questions posed by the title.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CME systems have failed to meet the needs of doctors in terms of their continuing professional development, and that the CPD diaries provide a more useful framework.

we need to develop and evaluate more flexible approaches to continuing education for doctors, and we must ensure that these approaches are based on a sound understanding of the adult learning process.
the CPD diaries are more likely to reflect the learning of public health doctors, whereas credit based CME systems are more likely to be the bureaucratic convenience of the Medical Royal Colleges.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to think carefully about the balance of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation for learning and about the role of credit based systems in continuing education.
the CME credit system does not seem to have a positive effect on the quality of CME.
we need to think carefully about what kind of continuing education we want and how we are going to get it.
